title: Water Management and Conservation
desc: Measure, save and manage water at home, farm, school or business, with leak checks, rainwater, reuse and fair sharing.
outcomes: Explain the water cycle and local water risks.
Do a water audit and leak test.
Judge quality, safety and cost of reuse.
Write a water-saving plan with targets.
task: Audit water use at one site, plan savings, design a rainwater or reuse option and set a measurable target.
condition: A real site or a practice case, a bucket and timer or meter, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor.
standard: Audit lists all uses in litres; leak test is documented; savings and payback are calculated; water safety rules are stated; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Facility managers, farmers, school staff, residents, community groups.
evidence: audit sheet, leak test record, plan, target
modules: Water cycle and local risk
Understand
Know where your water comes from and what could go wrong.
Sources: rain, rivers, lakes, groundwater and storage.
Risks: drought, flood, pollution and failing pipes.
Know your supplier, tariff, quality report and any local limits.
Storage can protect you during supply cuts.
A town cuts supply for three hours a day in summer. Households that store 150 litres per person cope; those that do not buy tanker water at five times the price.
Describe your water supply, its schedule and one risk with source.
Sources named; risk and storage size explained.
Water audit
Apply
Measure before you save.
Read the meter at the same time daily for a week.
List uses: taps, toilets, showers, cleaning, laundry, irrigation and leaks.
Convert to litres per person per day.
Compare with a benchmark from your supplier or national guidance (litres per person per day).
A household of five uses 900 litres a day: 180 per person. Garden use is 40 per cent in summer.
Complete a one-week audit and split indoor and outdoor use.
Table is complete and totals match the meter.
Finding and fixing leaks
Apply
Small leaks waste a lot.
Night meter test: stop all use; if the meter moves, there is a leak.
Dye test for toilets; check taps, hoses and float valves.
A drip per second wastes thousands of litres per year.
Measure flow by timing a bucket fill.
A toilet leak is found with food dye. A new valve saves about 20 litres a day. A float valve in a roof tank wasted 60 litres a day before it was adjusted.
Run a leak test and record results and fixes.
Result recorded with fix and saving.
Saving at the tap
Analyse
Cheap measures give quick savings.
Aerators, low-flow shower heads, efficient flushes and full loads.
Behaviour: shorter showers, tap off while brushing, reuse of rinse water.
Signs and feedback help.
Rank measures by litres saved per INR spent.
A low-flow shower head saves 6 litres per minute; an aerator cuts tap flow by 25 per cent.
Choose five measures and estimate savings.
Savings are estimated with numbers.
Rainwater harvesting
Create
Catch rain where it falls.
Roof area x rainfall x efficiency = litres per year.
Gutters, mesh, first-flush diverter, filter, covered tank and overflow route.
Use for non-drinking unless treated.
Clean the tank yearly.
A 100 m2 roof, 800 mm rain and 80 per cent efficiency give about 64,000 litres a year. A 5,000-litre tank fills after about 60 mm of rain.
Design a system with a calculation.
Calculation is correct and the design has overflow and cleaning.
Reuse and water quality
Evaluate
Grey water and treated water can be reused with care.
Grey water from basins and showers can irrigate non-edible plants where permitted.
Never use untreated grey water on salad crops.
A simple sand and gravel filter can help.
Test and treat drinking water; boil or disinfect if unsure.
A school filters hand-wash water and uses it for flushing toilets, cutting use by 20 per cent.
List safe and unsafe uses and a treatment step.
Rules are clear and a test is noted.
Irrigation and farming
Apply
Grow more with less.
Drip lines, mulching, timing and crop choice for local rain.
Water early morning or evening.
Check soil moisture with a finger or a simple sensor.
Group plants by water need.
Drip lines with mulch use about 40 per cent less water than flood irrigation and keep soil moist twice as long.
Plan a small plot with a watering timetable.
Plan is complete and justified.
Target, plan and progress
Create
Make saving a habit.
Set targets such as 20 per cent less in a year.
Assign owners and dates.
Display progress where everyone can see.
Report monthly and celebrate wins.
A school sets a 20 per cent cut in one year. A notice board shows monthly litres saved by class and the school reaches 17 per cent in the first six months.
Present the plan and progress display.
Target is measurable and the display is clear.
quiz: No use but meter moves means a leak.
rubric: Meter or bucket readings recorded for at least a week
Readings compared with a benchmark and the biggest use named
Abstraction, reuse and drinking-water rules for the place are written down
Rules checked with the local water body and a safe-use sign drafted
next: plastic alternatives, greenhouse gas auditing, vertical farming.
local: Water rights, rainwater and reuse rules differ by place.
ladder: Water cycle and local risk

L1: learner can name water sources. Focus module: Water cycle and local risk (Understand, 3 h). Know where your water comes from and what could go wrong. Key points: Sources: rain, rivers, lakes, groundwater and storage. Risks: drought, flood, pollution and failing pipes. Know your supplier, tariff, quality report and any local limits. Storage can protect you during supply cuts.

Teach: open with the worked example. A town cuts supply for three hours a day in summer. Households that store 150 litres per person cope; those that do not buy tanker water at five times the price. Then set the activity: Describe your water supply, its schedule and one risk with source. Mark against the standard: Sources named; risk and storage size explained. Check at this level: Name one local water risk. Model answer: Drought, flood, pollution or failing pipes.
Water audit

L2: learner knows leak basics. Focus module: Water audit (Apply, 5 h). Measure before you save. Key points: Read the meter at the same time daily for a week. List uses: taps, toilets, showers, cleaning, laundry, irrigation and leaks. Convert to litres per person per day. Compare with a benchmark from your supplier or national guidance (litres per person per day).

Teach: open with the worked example. A household of five uses 900 litres a day: 180 per person. Garden use is 40 per cent in summer. Then set the activity: Complete a one-week audit and split indoor and outdoor use. Mark against the standard: Table is complete and totals match the meter. Check at this level: Litres per person per day? Model answer: Total use / people / days.
Finding and fixing leaks

L3: learner can audit. Focus module: Finding and fixing leaks (Apply, 4 h). Small leaks waste a lot. Key points: Night meter test: stop all use; if the meter moves, there is a leak. Dye test for toilets; check taps, hoses and float valves. A drip per second wastes thousands of litres per year. Measure flow by timing a bucket fill.

Teach: open with the worked example. A toilet leak is found with food dye. A new valve saves about 20 litres a day. A float valve in a roof tank wasted 60 litres a day before it was adjusted. Then set the activity: Run a leak test and record results and fixes. Mark against the standard: Result recorded with fix and saving. Check at this level: Night meter test? Model answer: No use but meter moves means a leak.
Saving at the tap

L4: learner can fix and save. Focus module: Saving at the tap (Analyse, 4 h). Cheap measures give quick savings. Key points: Aerators, low-flow shower heads, efficient flushes and full loads. Behaviour: shorter showers, tap off while brushing, reuse of rinse water. Signs and feedback help. Rank measures by litres saved per rupee spent.

Teach: open with the worked example. A low-flow shower head saves 6 litres per minute; an aerator cuts tap flow by 25 per cent. Then set the activity: Choose five measures and estimate savings. Mark against the standard: Savings are estimated with numbers. Check at this level: Aerator benefit? Model answer: Reduces flow.
Rainwater harvesting

L5: learner can design rainwater. Focus module: Rainwater harvesting (Create, 5 h). Catch rain where it falls. Key points: Roof area x rainfall x efficiency = litres per year. Gutters, mesh, first-flush diverter, filter, covered tank and overflow route. Use for non-drinking unless treated. Clean the tank yearly.

Teach: open with the worked example. A 100 m2 roof, 800 mm rain and 80 per cent efficiency give about 64,000 litres a year. A 5,000-litre tank fills after about 60 mm of rain. Then set the activity: Design a system with a calculation. Mark against the standard: Calculation is correct and the design has overflow and cleaning. Check at this level: Rainwater formula? Model answer: Area x rain x efficiency.
Irrigation and farming

L6: learner can lead a plan. Focus module: Irrigation and farming (Apply, 3 h). Grow more with less. Key points: Drip lines, mulching, timing and crop choice for local rain. Water early morning or evening. Check soil moisture with a finger or a simple sensor. Group plants by water need.

Teach: open with the worked example. Drip lines with mulch use about 40 per cent less water than flood irrigation and keep soil moist twice as long. Then set the activity: Plan a small plot with a watering timetable. Mark against the standard: Plan is complete and justified. Check at this level: Mulch use? Model answer: Keeps moisture.
Target, plan and progress

L7: learner can audit others. Focus module: Target, plan and progress (Create, 4 h). Make saving a habit. Key points: Set targets such as 20 per cent less in a year. Assign owners and dates. Display progress where everyone can see. Report monthly and celebrate wins.

Teach: open with the worked example. A school sets a 20 per cent cut in one year. A notice board shows monthly litres saved by class and the school reaches 17 per cent in the first six months. Then set the activity: Present the plan and progress display. Mark against the standard: Target is measurable and the display is clear. Check at this level: Why share plan? Model answer: Community buy-in.
